Reasoning: When doing DC analysis, C1, C2, and CE are regarded as open circuits, and RL is DC-blocked by C2 and does not affect the DC operating point. If RB1 and RB2 are normal, the base voltage-divider voltage should be VB = 12×15/(105+15) = 1.5 V, and the measured VB = 1.4 V is very close to this, indicating that the base voltage-divider bias basically exists, and RB1 and RB2 are not very likely to be open-circuit. ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a voltage-divider biased common-emitter transistor amplifier circuit. RB1 is connected from +VCC to the base node, RB2 is connected from the base node to the bottom common ground; RC is connected from +VCC to the transistor collector; RE is connected from the emitter to ground, and CE is in parallel with RE as a bypass; C1 is the input coupling capacitor, C2 is the output coupling capacitor, and RL is connected from the output terminal to ground. Reasoning: When doing DC analysis, C1, C2, and CE are regarded as open circuits, and RL is DC-blocked by C2 and does not affect the DC operating point. If RB1 and RB2 are normal, the base voltage-divider voltage should be VB = 12×15/(105+15) = 1.5 V, and the measured VB = 1.4 V is very close to this, indicating that the base voltage-divider bias basically exists, and RB1 and RB2 are not very likely to be open-circuit. If the emitter DC loop is normal, when VB = 1.4 V, the emitter voltage should usually be about VE ≈ VB - 0.7 ≈ 0.7 V, and emitter/collector current will flow, causing a voltage drop on RC, so VC should be less than 12 V. Now the measured VE = 0 and VC = 12 V, indicating that there is basically no emitter current and collector current. The open-circuit fault that can cause the emitter to lose its DC loop while still keeping the base voltage-divider voltage close to normal is RE open-circuit.
